title: CLAUDE + SEEDANCE = The Creators Guide
key_takeaways: Generation is commoditized; the sellable skill is attaching a business problem to the asset — pitch a free one-month animated-asset test against a client's existing static email CTR baseline and convert the measured lift into a retainer.
Build the pipeline for yourself before you look for clients; the author's own path took 10 months from opening ChatGPT to inbound leads, entirely by testing and adjusting.

Every Seedance animation prompt in the guide follows the same skeleton: locked-off static camera, an explicit 'no hands, no objects, no people' exclusion, one specified light behaviour, exact preservation of the source image's colour grade, and 'end frame matches opening frame exactly' for a seamless loop.
Loopability is what makes an asset deployable — use start-frame and end-frame conditioning, and export all four aspect ratios (9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3) from the same session.
Light behaviour is the animation: drifting specular highlights, rotating hard key lights, and raking light that makes emboss depth legible do more work than moving the object.

Three ladder positions for an AI creator: sell standalone deployment-ready asset packages; bundle motion into existing branding work as 'standard'; or become an agency's white-label motion department, since most branding agencies do not offer motion at all.
Audio is the underrated half — Seedance 2.0 generates lip-synced dialogue, ambient, SFX and music natively, and harvesting audio across multiple generations enriches the final sound layer.

title: Seedance 2.0 Full Step-By-Step Guide + Advanced Techniques
key_takeaways: Seedance 2.0's differentiator is omni-reference: up to 9 images, 3 videos (15s total) and 3 audio files, 12 assets max, tagged @Image1/@Video1/@Audio1 and given an explicit role in the prompt — an untagged asset is used ambiguously.

Use the timestamp method: break the video into 4–5 second blocks and give each one both its dialogue line and its exact visual blocking; the model follows instructions literally, so under-specifying is the main failure mode.

Extend rather than regenerate — re-upload your finished clip as @Video1 and prompt an extension with 'keep the voice the same as the original clip'; three extensions yields 45–60 seconds with continuous character, voice and environment.
Voice-ID referencing beats generating audio from scratch: upload real extracted audio and instruct the model to use it purely as a voice identity reference while speaking your own dialogue.

Beat the 2000-character prompt limit by rendering the full detailed prompt as text in a Canva image, uploading it as a reference, and prompting 'transcribe this image and use the movements described here.'

Starting-image quality is inherited — use JSON colour-grading prompts in Nano Banana Pro to avoid the grey AI look, and reverse-engineer JSON prompts from screenshotted TikTok frames in your niche so the first frame already matches what performs there.
Because the model is ByteDance-trained it adds cuts, transitions and short-form pacing unprompted, which collapses post-production to arranging 3–5 clips plus captions.
Upscale at 2x/60fps in Topaz then export at 30fps — 60fps in the final social deliverable looks wrong.

title: The Complete Guide to Building an AI UGC That Makes Money – Using Seedance 2.0 on Higgsfield
key_takeaways: Character consistency is the growth variable: generate a 9-pose reference grid in Nano-Banana (front, three-quarter left/right, profile, up, down, smiling, serious, mid-action) and use it as the master reference on every generation — without it the face drifts and follow-through quietly drops.

Prompt the face with concrete attributes — age range, body type, setting, mood, lighting direction — because '28-year-old wellness creator in morning light' is usable where 'a beautiful woman' is not.

The cost argument, not the novelty, is the case: $2K–$10K per human influencer partnership with weeks of negotiation versus roughly $37/month for a character you own and can direct on your own schedule.

Account-growth rules the author tested: fresh account only (repurposed accounts get throttled), 2-day algorithmic warm-up before the first post, ramp 1 → 2 → 3–4 reels per day, and no bio link for the first 30 days.
Comment-to-DM automation from day 1 does double duty — it manufactures the engagement signal the algorithm rewards while routing warm traffic to the product link.

Stack six revenue streams from week 1 rather than waiting on one brand deal; affiliate and comment-to-DM sales work at any follower count, brand inbound starts around 5K engaged followers, and character IP licensing is the passive tail.
Cited demand data: nearly 1 in 3 Gen Z consumers have bought on an AI influencer's recommendation, rising to 47% among 19–21 year olds.

title: The Seedance 2.0 Prompting Bible
key_takeaways: Order the prompt subject > action > camera > style > constraints: subject pins a centre of gravity, action is the kinetic anchor, camera locks framing before the model re-decides the lens, style comes late so it does not hijack motion, constraints close the remaining gaps.

Write directions, not states — 'she slowly turns toward the camera, breeze lifting the hem of her skirt' executes as a sequence where 'she looks happy' only gives the model a photograph to approximate.
Always split subject motion from camera motion into two separate clauses; fused phrasing like 'spinning camera around a dancing person' is the actual cause of most output people blame on the model.

Lighting description has the largest single effect on output quality per the official Volcengine guide — if you add only one thing to a weak prompt, add lighting; 'golden hour' is the highest quality-per-word gain.

Describe camera rhythm (slow, gentle, smooth) rather than f-stops, ISO or millimetres, use one primary movement per generation, and sequence compound moves into temporal phases instead of stacking them.

Banned-word list: 'fast' unqualified, bare 'cinematic', 'epic', 'amazing/beautiful/stunning', 'lots of movement', and 'glow/glimmer/glints' (which induce specular flicker) — the rule is that any word describing how the viewer should feel forces the model to guess a visual and it guesses wrong.

Positive constraint phrasing beats negative prompt syntax: 'avoid jitter', 'avoid bent limbs' (in every character prompt), 'avoid identity drift', 'maintain face consistency', plus the standard suffix 'sharp clarity, natural colors, stable picture, no blur, no ghosting, no flickering'.

Untagged reference files get averaged into mush — give every upload an explicit @ role; the first-last frame trick (@Image1 opening frame, @Image2 closing frame) gets coherent interpolated motion with no storyboarding.
Iterate one variable per pass and score for continuity and adherence; rewriting the whole prompt after a failure makes the cause unidentifiable.

title: Seedance 2.0: The New Default Video Model
key_takeaways: The real shift is the input shape, not the model — previous models made you pick text or image; Seedance V2 combines up to two images, two videos and an audio file in one tagged prompt, which turns generating into directing.

Treat it as an editor as well as a generator: a green-screen clip plus two character references plus a background image, with an instruction to preserve motion exactly, replaced a studio shoot day in about 60 seconds.

Everything starts with a very good source image — words make the model guess, a reference that matches your taste makes it stop guessing; supply a clean face reference, a background carrying the lighting and composition you want, and a video where the motion is already right.

The prompt-length rule inverts from Kling 3: shorter wins on Kling, longer and more specific wins on Seedance V2, especially for character identity, motion fidelity from a reference video, and scene transitions.
Use an LLM-in-the-loop: draft the prompt yourself, have an LLM optimize it, then generate — the lesson is the loop, not which model you pick.

Match model to job on fidelity, speed and cost per output: Seedance V2 as daily driver for ads, logos, UX animation and influencer content; Kling 3 for cinematic emotion; Enhancer V4 deliberately lower-fidelity for talking heads.
Adobe's remaining ground is finishing, not generating — 8K output, frame-level edits, and fixing the parts the model got not-quite-right; the workflow is generate in Seedance, finish in Adobe, ship.

Three demoed money use cases all remove logistics rather than creative work: virtual try-on with zero shipped product, AI-influencer reviews of products nobody touched, and green-screen character/background replacement instead of a reshoot.

title: Output isn't design
key_takeaways: The hard part of design is rarely generating the form — it is understanding the problem well enough to know what and how something should exist at all; tools that promise faster interface generation mistake producing for designing.

Uses Alexander's Notes on the Synthesis of Form: design is the search for a good fit between form and context, where context is the full set of forces making the problem what it is — needs, technical constraints, conflicting requirements, habits, edge cases, and relationships you only notice after spending time with them.
Bad design is where those forces stay unresolved; good design is where the misfits have been worked through carefully.

AI's failure mode is generating plausible output instead of first shaping the problem — the visible symptom is products that look polished and ambitious but unravel on use: brittle, poorly integrated, full of decisions never worked through. 'The form is there. The fit is not.'

Working visually is defended as a thinking method, not a preference: moving things around, testing relationships and refining structure is part of how clarity emerges, and it is slow enough to leave room to think.
The writing analogy: writing clarifies thought because the act forces you to organize it, and having AI write for you produces text without rearranging your thinking — design behaves the same way.
AI remains useful for prototyping, exploring and surprising you, but design still requires judgment, conversation, tension and time.
The stated risk is mistaking generated form for solved problems.
